title: the birth of the cousins
hook: a forest sage with blazing eyes comes to a palace bedroom, a frightened widow shuts her eyes, and a son is born blind
carry: a widow too frightened to look

segments.voice: Last week ended with Satyavati thinking of her firstborn, and Vyasa appearing at once — she thinks of him; he comes. Did you send someone a word? Day seven hundred twenty-two.

Vyasa comes to the palace straight from the forest, and he looks it. He has lived there practicing austerities, and the text describes him: dark skin, matted hair the color of copper, a rough beard, eyes that blaze, the text says, and a smell no one would call perfume. His mother has asked him to give the house of the Kurus a son. He agrees. And he asks that they wait first. Satyavati answers: there is no time.
screen: `A SAGE FROM THE FOREST.` → `HE ASKS FOR TIME.` → `THERE IS NO TIME.`

segments.voice: This begins a new part of the serial: the birth of the cousins. Over the next days, the princes of the Kuru house come into the world: first the fathers, then the cousins who will one day face each other across a battlefield. And it starts here, with an ancient custom: when a man died without children, a learned man could be invited to father them in his name, so the line would go on. That's what Satyavati is asking. Vyasa says the widows should first keep a vow for a while, to be ready. Satyavati says the kingdom can't wait for a king. So Vyasa says: then let the princess bear my looks, my smell, my grim face. That will be her vow. Satyavati goes to the elder widow, Ambika, and tells her that a brother-in-law will come to her tonight. Ambika thinks of the heroes of the Kuru house, and waits. The lamp is lit. And in comes Vyasa, with his blazing eyes and copper hair. She's afraid, and she shuts her eyes, and keeps them shut. Afterward Vyasa tells his mother: the son will be strong and wise, a fine prince. But because his mother closed her eyes, he will be born blind. And Satyavati answers at once: a blind man can't be king of the Kurus. Give the family another. That son is Dhritarashtra. The poem lets us see how it starts: with a widow too frightened to look, a mother in a hurry, and a son who will spend his whole life near a throne he can't fully have. Vyasa ties the blindness to her closed eyes, but the text doesn't make her a villain. It shows what fear did in one night, and lets the consequences unfold.
screen: `AN OLD CUSTOM FOR A LINE.` · `NO TIME TO WAIT.` · `AMBIKA SHUTS HER EYES.` · `DHRITARASHTRA, BORN BLIND.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come and go. Ambika closed her eyes because she was afraid, and the story turned on it. Bring to mind something you've been not looking at: a bill, a test result, a conversation, a feeling. Don't open it now. Just turn toward it a little, inside, the way you'd turn toward a sound in the next room. Notice the fear, if it's there. Breathe in beside it. Breathe out, and keep your inner eyes open one moment longer. The bell holds the time.
Dhritarashtra, born blind because his mother, Ambika, couldn't bear to look at the sage who fathered him for the house of the Kurus.
Your line: a widow too frightened to look. Today, look straight at one thing you've been shutting your eyes to, even for a minute. Day seven hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: The ancient custom in this story, called niyoga, is described in old texts and the epics; it is not practiced in Hindu families today, and the story is told for what it shows about the Kuru line.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Vyasa's request that the widows first observe a vow (the text gives a length, left out here under the claims rule); Satyavati's insistence; Vyasa's description of his own appearance and smell as the princess's 'vow'; Ambika thinking of Kuru heroes; her closing her eyes; Vyasa's prediction of a strong, wise son born blind; Satyavati's reply.
The text's specific comparisons of Dhritarashtra's strength (numbers of elephants) and its count of his future sons are left out under the claims rule.
Niyoga and consent are sensitive for modern listeners; the script stays plain and does not describe the night. A Keeper may wish to adjust.
The new part's framing ('princes who will one day face each other across a battlefield') anticipates the war in general terms only.
howItsDone says niyoga is not practiced today; confirm phrasing.
